acts.title: Text A · The Welsh in Patagonia
text: In 1865 a ship called the Mimosa left Liverpool with a hundred and fifty-three passengers on board. They were going to Patagonia, in the south of Argentina, and the plan was not to make a fortune. The plan was to keep a language.

Welsh was under pressure at home, and the settlers had been promised land where they could run their own schools, their own chapels and their own courts. What they had not been told was that the land was almost desert.
The community very nearly failed in the first winter. It survived because the Tehuelche, the people already living there, taught the newcomers where the water was and how to hunt.

A hundred and sixty years later the descendants are Argentinian citizens. Around fifty thousand of them have Welsh ancestry, and several thousand still speak the language. The chapels are still standing, and the singing festival is still held every year.

items.q: Why did the settlers leave for Patagonia?
o: To keep their language and run their own institutions

items.q: Why did the community survive the first winter?
o: The Tehuelche taught them where water was and how to hunt

acts.title: Text B · The Icelanders in Manitoba
text: Gimli is a small town on the shore of Lake Winnipeg, and it holds the largest concentration of people of Icelandic descent anywhere outside Iceland.

The first settlers arrived in 1875, after a volcano had destroyed the farmland they depended on. They were given a strip of land nobody else wanted, and for four years they governed it themselves, with their own written constitution and their own newspaper.
The community assimilated, as almost all of them do. Icelandic stopped being a language of the home somewhere around the third generation, and most residents of Gimli today speak only English.

What survived was the festival. Every August the town holds a ceremony and a parade, people dress in Viking costume, and a few thousand visitors arrive. Heritage, it turns out, is easier to preserve as an event than as a language.

items.s: Gimli has the largest Icelandic community outside Iceland.
The settlers left Iceland because of a volcano.
They governed the settlement themselves for a period.
items.why: They did — for four years, with their own constitution. Read that sentence again.

items.s: Most people in Gimli today speak Icelandic at home.
The August festival includes a parade and Viking costume.
The writer suggests a festival is easier to keep alive than a language.

items.q: “a ship called the Mimosa” — why a and then the?
o: a for the first mention; the with the name, which is unique

items.q: “Welsh was under pressure” — why no article?
o: It is a proper noun so it takes the

items.q: “Heritage is easier to preserve” — why no article?
o: An uncountable noun used in a general sense takes none
the was left out by mistake

items.q: “the largest concentration” — why the?
o: A superlative points to one thing only

acts.title: Articles at B2: the four decisions
rule: English makes you decide something about every noun you write. The decision is not really about a, the or nothing — it is about two questions asked in order. First: is this one of many, or the one we both mean? Second: is it countable, and is it singular?
points: One of many, mentioned for the first time, singular and countable. A ship left Liverpool.
We both know which one. Because it was mentioned before, because there is only one, or because the sentence itself identifies it.
Plurals and uncountables used in a general sense; languages, most countries, meals, and institutions seen as an idea.
the with superlatives and unique things
the largest concentration, the sun, the government, the Mimosa.
at school vs at the school
With institutions, no article means the idea; the means the building.
eg: A ship left Liverpool in 1865.
First mention, one of many.
The ship was called the Mimosa.
Second mention — now we both know which ship.
Welsh was under pressure at home.
Languages take no article.
Heritage is easier to preserve as an event.
Uncountable, general sense.
Settlers arrived in 1875.
Plural, general sense — no article.
The settlers who arrived in 1875 governed themselves.
the, because the relative clause identifies exactly which settlers.
It is the largest community outside Iceland.
Superlative — there is only one.
She is at university in Buenos Aires.
The institution as an idea.
Meet me at the university at four.
The building.
The Netherlands, the United States, the Philippines.
A few countries take the — the plural and “united” ones.
acts.careful: A relative clause often turns a into the: “a language” becomes “the language they wanted to keep”. If the sentence itself tells the reader which one, use the.

write.q: Write about 180 words on a community in your country that came from somewhere else, or on a custom your own family has kept. Say when it was established, what has survived and what has not. Watch your articles: check every singular countable noun before you finish.
plan: who they were and when they arrived
write.model:
There is a village about an hour north of Karaganda that was built by families deported from the Volga in 1941. They arrived in October with what they could carry, which in most cases was not much.

The community was established properly within about five years, and by the 1960s it had a school, a clinic and a reputation for growing things nobody else could grow in that soil.

What has survived is the food and the graveyard. There is a bakery in Karaganda run by a great-grandson, and the bread is exactly what his grandmother made, down to the shape.

What has not survived is the language. It stopped being spoken at home in the third generation, and the last fluent speaker in that village died about ten years ago.

What is unusual is that nobody there considers any of this remarkable. Ask about the history and you get directions to the bakery.
